newsitem.title: USA: New CRP rules likely next week - USDA's Glickman.
newsitem.headline: New CRP rules likely next week - USDA's Glickman.

text.p: The new set of rules for the Conservation Reserve "more than likely" will be unveiled next week, U.S. Agriculture Secretary Dan Glickman said Tuesday.

In an impromptu interview with Reuters, Glickman rebutted critics who feared the new rules would be too lax and let in land that was not environmentally fragile. He declined to discuss the regulations, which need White House budget-office approval, in detail.
"I think they're wrong," Glickman said of critics. "The fact of the matter is the focus of this program will be on highly erodible land...and will be in the way we implement it."

Created in 1985, the reserve pays farmers an annual rent for taking fragile land out of production for 10 years. About 36.4 million acres were enrolled in the reserve, making it the largest long-term U.S. land retirement program ever.
"It (the new rule) will more than likely be out next week. We're pushing it as fast as we can," Glickman said. "The (White House budget office) has to approve the final rule."

Implementation of the new rules will be a key test, Glickman said, because far more land would be eligible than could be accepted. The Agrculture Department has estimated 120 million acres could meet eligibility criteria proposed last fall.
"So we are going to have to be prudent and careful in terms of how we make decisions," Glickman said. "We've got good local people on the ground who will be capable of doing that."
Norm Berg, a soil conservation activist, said it was vital to put the new rules into effect soon so farmers could decide whether to submit a bid to enroll their land.
Contracts on 24 million acres in the reserve were due to expire this fall. Some eight million acres now enrolled would not meet the erodibility threshhold proposed last fall.
While conservationists fretted the new rules would be too lax, some lawmakers feared a bias against Plains states.
